items.q: Which term matches this description?
items.stimulus: Name for the large land-based empires of about 1450 to 1750 that used cannons and muskets to conquer neighbors and hold their land.
items.why: Your worksheet names Russia, the Mughals, the Ottomans and the Safavids. Many historians count only the three Islamic ones.

items.q: Which term matches this description?
items.stimulus: Machine with movable metal type built in Germany around 1450 that made books cheaper and helped ideas spread quickly across Europe.
items.why: It is one of the events that marks the start of the early modern period.

items.q: Who were the four Gunpowder Empires?
items.answer: Russia, the Mughal Empire, the Ottoman Empire and the Safavid Empire.
items.why: That is the worksheet's list. Many historians count only the three Islamic ones (Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal), but teach the four on your worksheet.

items.q: Why did the Gunpowder Empires craft artistic and architectural legacies?
items.answer: To show off the ruler's power, wealth and right to rule, and to glorify their religion.
items.why: Grand mosques, palaces and paintings told subjects and rivals that the ruler was strong and legitimate.

items.q: What did Europe's expansion involve that was unique from the Gunpowder Empires?
items.answer: Europeans expanded overseas by sea, building colonies and trade networks across oceans, while the Gunpowder Empires grew over land.
items.why: Gunpowder empires were land-based. Europe's new empires crossed the Atlantic and Indian Oceans.

items.q: What is significant about the year 1450?
items.answer: It is about when the early modern period begins, as the Gutenberg printing press appears and the Ottomans are about to take Constantinople.
items.why: Historians use the mid-1400s as the dividing line between the medieval period and the early modern period.

items.q: What events signal the beginning of the early modern period (the mid-1450s)?
items.answer: The Ottoman capture of Constantinople in 1453 and the invention of the Gutenberg printing press around 1450.
items.why: The 1453 fall of Constantinople ended the Byzantine Empire, and printing spread ideas faster than ever.
items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: Monarchies in Europe in 1450 wanted to control:
items.answer: Taxes, trade and their powerful nobles, so they could build stronger central governments.
items.why: Kings wanted money and armies they controlled, instead of depending on nobles.
items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: Which social class was becoming more powerful in Europe?
items.answer: The merchant (middle) class, who grew rich from trade and banking.
items.why: Trade made merchants wealthy, and kings often allied with them against the old nobility.
items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: Which term matches this description?
items.stimulus: Russian ruler of the 1500s, the first to be crowned tsar, nicknamed 'the Terrible', who conquered Kazan and Astrakhan and pushed Russia's border east.
items.why: His conquests opened the Volga River and the road to Siberia.

items.q: Which term matches this description?
items.stimulus: Longest river in Europe, flowing south into the Caspian Sea, and a key trade route that Russia wanted to control.
items.why: Controlling it gave Russia trade with Central Asia and Persia.

items.q: Which two regions was Russia influenced by?
items.answer: Europe and Asia.
items.why: Russia sits across both, with Orthodox Christian and Byzantine ties to the west and Mongol rule from the east.

items.q: How did Ivan IV extend the border of Russia eastward?
items.answer: He conquered the Tatar khanates of Kazan and Astrakhan using gunpowder weapons, which opened the way into Siberia.
items.why: Muskets and cannons gave his army the edge over the Tatar forces.

items.q: What did Russia's expansion depend on?
items.answer: Gunpowder weapons and the Cossacks who fought for the tsar.
items.why: Firearms let small Russian forces beat larger groups in Siberia.
items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: Who were the Cossacks and what did they do?
items.answer: Free warrior-settlers of the steppe frontier who served the Russian tsars as soldiers and explorers and helped conquer Siberia.
items.why: They pushed the border east and guarded it.

items.q: Why did Russia want to control the Volga River?
items.answer: It was a major trade route, so controlling it gave Russia trade with Central Asia and Persia and access to the Caspian Sea.
items.why: Whoever held the Volga controlled the flow of goods across that region.

items.q: What religion did Russian missionaries want to convert Siberian tribes to?
items.answer: Eastern Orthodox Christianity.
items.why: Russia's rulers tied their state to the Russian Orthodox Church.

items.q: Where did the Russian Empire extend to by 1639?
items.answer: Across Siberia to the Pacific Ocean.
items.why: Russian explorers reached the Pacific coast in 1639. Alaska came much later, in the 1700s.

items.q: Which term matches this description?
items.stimulus: Chinese ruling family that took power in 1368 after driving out the Mongols and kept China stable for about 300 years.
items.why: They rebuilt the Great Wall and restored Chinese rule.

items.q: Which term matches this description?
items.stimulus: Last ruling family of China, set up by Manchus from the northeast, which took over China in 1644 and greatly enlarged its territory.
items.why: It replaced the Ming and ruled until 1912.

items.q: Which term matches this description?
items.stimulus: Qing emperor who ruled 61 years (to 1722), the longest reign in Chinese history, and brought Taiwan, Mongolia and Tibet under Qing control.
items.why: His long, steady rule made the Qing strong and larger.

items.q: Which term matches this description?
items.stimulus: Qing emperor of the late 1700s who pushed the empire into Central Asia and Tibet, but whose last years brought corruption and money trouble.
items.why: The empire peaked under him, then began to weaken.

items.q: The Ming Dynasty was established after the Mongols were pushed out of China. What was the result of the Ming Dynasty?
items.answer: Chinese rule was restored, and China enjoyed about 300 years of stability and prosperity.
items.why: The Ming ruled from 1368 to 1644 and rebuilt the Great Wall.

items.q: Who established the Qing Dynasty?
items.answer: The Manchus, from Manchuria.
items.why: They took Beijing in 1644 after the Ming collapsed.

items.q: What caused China to rebuild the Great Wall of China for protection?
items.answer: The threat of Mongol raids from the north.
items.why: The Ming rebuilt it in stone and brick to keep Mongol invaders out.

items.q: What was significant about Emperor Kangxi's rule AND what regions did he incorporate into China's rule?
items.answer: He had the longest reign in Chinese history (61 years) and brought Taiwan, Mongolia and Tibet into Qing rule.
items.why: A long reign gave the Qing stability while the empire grew.

items.q: What was notable about Emperor Qianlong's rule? (where did he expand, what was the reaction to his expansion, etc.)
items.answer: He expanded Qing rule into Central Asia and Tibet, which made the empire its largest, but the wars were costly and not every campaign worked.
accept: expanded into central asia and tibet
items.why: The empire reached its peak under him.
items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: Were the following expansion efforts by China successful or unsuccessful: Tibet, Burma, Vietnam?
items.answer: Tibet: successful. Burma: unsuccessful. Vietnam: unsuccessful.
accept: tibet successful burma and vietnam unsuccessful
items.why: Qing armies held Tibet but failed against Burma (1765 to 1769) and Vietnam (1788 to 1789).

items.q: What was the result of these efforts to expand?
items.answer: The Qing Empire grew to its largest size, but the long wars were expensive and strained its money.
items.why: Big conquests brought land but also heavy costs.
items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: Describe the late years of Emperor Qianlong's reign.
items.answer: The government became corrupt, money problems grew, and unrest rose, as shown by favorites like Heshen who stole from the state.
items.why: His final years began the Qing decline.

items.q: Why was the White Lotus Society reinstated? Where have we heard of them before?
items.answer: Poverty, heavy taxes and corrupt officials made people rebel. They were also behind a rebellion against the Mongol Yuan dynasty, which led to the Ming.
items.why: The White Lotus was a Buddhist-inspired secret society that rebelled in hard times.
items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: What was the result of their uprising?
items.answer: The Qing crushed it after about eight years (1796 to 1804), with some 100,000 rebels killed, and it badly weakened the dynasty.
items.why: The costs showed how weak the Qing had become.

items.q: Which term matches this description?
items.stimulus: Turkic-Mongol conqueror of the late 1300s, ruling from Samarkand, who conquered Persia, Central Asia and Delhi but left no lasting government.
items.why: His empire fell apart soon after his death in 1405.

items.q: Which term matches this description?
items.stimulus: Belief that a Muslim warrior who fights to spread and defend Islam deserves honor, which inspired fighters to expand the early Ottoman state.
items.why: It gave conquest a religious purpose and a loyal army.

items.q: What did the Gunpowder Empires have in common?
items.answer: They used gunpowder weapons, strong armies and strong rulers to conquer and control large territories.
items.why: Cannons and muskets helped central rulers beat rivals.

items.q: What made the Gunpowder Empires successful?
items.answer: Gunpowder weapons, strong armies, and strong rulers with organized governments.
items.why: Guns, big armies and good administrators let them hold huge lands.
items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: Who was Tamerlane and where did he conquer?
items.answer: A Turkic-Mongol conqueror (1336 to 1405) who ruled from Samarkand and conquered Persia, Central Asia, parts of India and the Middle East.
items.why: He even defeated the Ottomans at Ankara in 1402.

items.q: How did the Ghazi Ideal help the Gunpowder Empires grow?
items.answer: It gave warriors a religious reason to fight and spread Islam, which built loyal armies and justified conquest.
items.why: Fighting for the faith made soldiers eager and rulers legitimate.

items.q: Conquests led by the Gunpowder Empires were marked by what?
items.answer: Violence and destruction, though later rulers often ruled their new lands more tolerantly.
items.why: Tamerlane in particular was known for massacres.
items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: How did Tamerlane encourage the arts?
items.answer: He brought skilled artists and builders from conquered lands to Samarkand and built grand mosques and buildings.
items.why: The fine buildings of Samarkand showed his power.

items.q: Tamerlane's invasions were a testament to what?
items.answer: The power of fast nomadic cavalry armies and strong military leadership.
items.why: His conquests relied on horsemen and skilled command, not mainly on guns.
items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: Tamerlane's government depended on what?
items.answer: His personal leadership and his army.
items.why: With no lasting system, it needed him to hold it together.
items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: How did Tamerlane fail?
items.answer: He did not build a lasting government, so his empire split apart among his heirs after he died in 1405.
accept: empire fell apart after his death
items.why: Rule by one man's strength did not outlive him.

items.q: Which two major forces would continue to battle with each other into the 14th century?
items.answer: The Ottoman (Sunni) and Safavid (Shia) empires, who fought for centuries.
items.why: The worksheet says 14th century, which is probably a typo, since the Safavids only began in 1501. The two empires fought from 1514 into the 1700s.
items.note: The worksheet wording is odd (the 14th century is too early for these empires), so the intended answer is a best guess.

items.q: Which term matches this description?
items.stimulus: Muslim empire that began in Anatolia around 1300, took Constantinople in 1453 and ruled southeast Europe, the Middle East and North Africa until 1922.
items.why: It was one of the largest and longest-lasting Islamic empires.

items.q: Which term matches this description?
items.stimulus: Ottoman sultan nicknamed 'the Conqueror' who captured Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire.
items.why: He made Constantinople the Ottoman capital.

items.q: Which term matches this description?
items.stimulus: Ottoman sultan (1520 to 1566), called 'the Magnificent', who led the empire at its height and besieged Vienna in 1529.
items.why: Under him the empire peaked in size, wealth and art.

items.q: Where was the Ottoman Empire located?
items.answer: In Anatolia (modern Turkey), stretching across southeast Europe, the Middle East and North Africa.
items.why: It sat where Europe, Asia and Africa meet.

items.q: Why is the Ottoman Empire significant?
items.answer: It was one of the largest and longest-lasting Islamic empires (about 1300 to 1922) and controlled key trade routes between Europe, Asia and Africa.
items.why: It also ended the Byzantine Empire in 1453.

items.q: Under Mehmed II, where was the capital city of the Ottoman Empire?
items.answer: Constantinople (today's Istanbul), the old Byzantine capital.
items.why: He captured it in 1453.

items.q: Why was the location of the capital city significant?
items.answer: It sat on the strait between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, where Europe meets Asia, so the Ottomans controlled key trade routes.
items.why: It was a perfect spot for trade and defense.
items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: What was the Ottoman relationship with Venice?
items.answer: They were rivals who fought wars over the Mediterranean, but also trading partners.
items.why: Venice fought several wars with the Ottomans but still wanted to trade with them.
items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: Why was Suleiman I's siege of Vienna significant?
items.answer: It was the farthest the Ottomans pushed into central Europe in 1529, and they failed to take the city.
items.why: Your worksheet says Venice, but Suleiman's famous siege was of Vienna in 1529.

items.q: What led to the eventual fall of the Ottoman Empire in 1922?
items.answer: The empire's defeat in World War I, after which the Allies occupied it and Turkish nationalists ended the sultanate in 1922.
items.why: It was World War I (1914 to 1918). The empire was gone before World War II began.

src.label: Wikipedia: Dissolution of the Ottoman Empire

items.q: Which term matches this description?
items.stimulus: Persian title for a king, used by the rulers of Iran such as the Safavid leaders.
items.why: The Safavid shahs held both political and religious authority.

items.q: Which term matches this description?
items.stimulus: Empire founded in 1501 in Iran by Ismail I that made Shia Islam the state religion and clashed with the Sunni Ottomans.
items.why: Its religion still shapes Iran today.

items.q: Which term matches this description?
items.stimulus: Safavid ruler (1588 to 1629) who built a strong army with cannons and muskets, moved the capital to Isfahan and boosted trade.
items.why: Under him the empire reached its height.

items.q: What was the origin of the Safavid Empire?
items.answer: It began in 1501 when Ismail I, leader of the Safavid Sufi order, conquered Iran and made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion.
items.why: The Safavids had been a religious order before they became rulers.

items.q: List two problems the Safavid Empire faced.
items.answer: Constant wars with the Ottomans, and a weak navy and little access to the sea.
items.why: The Sunni Ottomans pressed from the west, and tribal rivalries also caused trouble.
items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: How did Europe assist the Safavid Empire?
items.answer: European advisers (such as the English Sherley brothers, according to traditional accounts) helped train and arm the Safavid army, since Europe also wanted an ally against the Ottomans.
items.why: Shah Abbas I used Western help to modernize his army.
items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: Safavid shahs controlled what two things?
items.answer: Overland trade routes such as the Silk Road, and the silk trade.
items.why: Their land sat between Europe and Asia, which brought wealth.
items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book. Your book may say political and religious power instead.

items.q: What two things caused tension between the Safavid and Ottoman Empires?
items.answer: Religion (Shia versus Sunni) and rivalry over land and trade routes.
items.why: The Ottomans were Sunni and the Safavids Shia, and both wanted the same lands.
items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: How did the Ottomans try to assert dominance over the Safavid Empire?
items.answer: They defeated the Safavids in battle (Chaldiran, 1514) and also cut off trade with them.
items.why: The Ottomans had better artillery and also used trade bans.
items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: Describe the place of women in the Safavid Empire.
items.answer: Upper-class women could be educated and have political influence, and women could own property and travel, but their freedom shrank after Shah Abbas I.
items.why: Women had real roles early on, but later shahs placed more limits on them.
items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: Which term matches this description?
items.stimulus: Mughal emperor of the late 1500s who expanded the empire across northern India and won Hindu support by tolerating other religions.
items.why: His fair policies helped hold the empire together.

items.q: Which term matches this description?
items.stimulus: Muslim empire that ruled most of India from 1526 until the 1700s, famous for its wealth and for the Taj Mahal.
items.why: It blended Persian, Islamic and Indian culture.

items.q: Which term matches this description?
items.stimulus: Hereditary social group in India that decides a person's job and who they can marry, passed down from parents.
items.why: Caste shaped daily life in Hindu India.

items.q: What was significant about the Mughal Empire?
items.answer: It was one of the richest and most powerful empires, uniting most of India under Muslim rulers and blending Muslim and Hindu cultures.
items.why: It ruled a huge, wealthy population.

items.q: What was the role of Arab traders in the Mughal Empire?
items.answer: They carried goods across the Indian Ocean, helping Mughal commerce by trading Indian goods abroad.
items.why: Muslim merchants linked India to Arabia, Africa and Southeast Asia.

src.label: Wikipedia: Economy of the Mughal Empire

items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: What goods were imported and exported in the Mughal Empire?
items.answer: Imported silver (and horses); exported cotton textiles, spices and other goods.
items.why: Foreign traders paid in silver for Indian cloth.

src.label: Wikipedia: Economy of the Mughal Empire

items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: What were the Hindu castes?
items.answer: Social groups you are born into: Brahmins (priests), Kshatriyas (warriors and rulers), Vaishyas (merchants) and Shudras (laborers).
items.why: People outside the four groups were treated as lowest and were often left out.

items.q: Why is the architecture of the Mughal Empire significant?
items.answer: Buildings like the Taj Mahal blended Persian, Islamic and Indian styles and showed the empire's wealth and power.
items.why: Mughal architecture shows both their wealth and their cultural mix.

items.q: Why did the Gunpowder Empires decline?
items.answer: Weak rulers, corruption and rebellions inside, and falling behind Europe in military technology and industry.
items.why: Europe kept improving its armies and economy while these empires stayed the same.

src.label: Wikipedia: Decline and modernization of the Ottoman Empire

items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: Why did Russia remain despite the other Gunpowder Empires falling?
items.answer: Russia modernized and copied western Europe, starting with Peter the Great, and kept a strong central government.
items.why: Russia adopted western armies and technology.
items.note: This answer depends on how the AMSCO textbook words it, so check it against your book.

items.q: Summarize why the Ottoman Empire eventually declined.
items.answer: Weak sultans, corruption, loss of military edge, and economic trouble as European powers grew stronger.
items.why: Europeans pulled ahead in technology and trade.

src.label: Wikipedia: Decline and modernization of the Ottoman Empire

items.q: What were 'Harem Politics' and how did they contribute to the fall of the Ottoman Empire?
items.answer: Wives and mothers of sultans fought to put their own sons on the throne, which gave the empire weak, inexperienced rulers.
items.why: Some historians call this period the Sultanate of Women.

items.q: Summarize why the Safavid Empire declined.
items.answer: After Shah Abbas I, weaker shahs, rebellions and pressure from neighbors broke it down, ending with an Afghan invasion in 1722.
items.why: The Afghan capture of Isfahan in 1722 is often called the end.

items.q: Summarize why the Mughal Empire declined.
items.answer: Costly wars and religious intolerance under Aurangzeb, revolts, corruption and weak successors, and growing European (British) power.
items.why: By the 1700s the empire had shrunk to a shadow of itself.

src.label: Wikipedia: Decline of the Mughal Empire
